cards.front: Which enzyme converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, and where is it mainly found?
cards.back: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), a dipeptidyl carboxypeptidase on the luminal surface of endothelial cells, especially in the lungs. Ang I is only about one hundredth as potent as Ang II, so this conversion is the key activation step.

cards.front: Classify: sites of renin-angiotensin system inhibition
cards.text: {{Beta-blockers}} reduce renin release; {{aliskiren}} blocks renin itself; {{ACE inhibitors}} block Ang I to Ang II conversion; {{ARBs}} block the AT1 receptor; {{spironolactone}} blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor.

cards.front: Angiotensin (1-7): how it is formed and what it does
cards.back: Formed from Ang I or Ang II by ACE 2; acts on the Mas receptor to cause NO-dependent vasodilatation, antithrombotic and antiproliferative effects. ACE inhibitors raise its level by diverting Ang I.

cards.front: Angiotensin IV: receptor and effect
cards.back: Hexapeptide (Ang 3-8) acting on the AT4 receptor, which is insulin-regulated aminopeptidase (IRAP); it prevents breakdown of neuropeptides involved in memory; improves memory in animals.

cards.front: Angiotensin III: potency compared with Ang II
cards.back: Heptapeptide that is 2 to 10 times less potent than Ang II, but equipotent in stimulating aldosterone secretion.

cards.front: Prorenin and the (pro)renin receptor: why they matter
cards.back: Prorenin circulates at 5 to 10 times renin levels and is active in its own right. Binding to the PRR augments its activity reversibly, and tissue activation drives local RAS effects (Ang II-dependent and independent pathways). Prorenin to renin ratio rises in diabetes.

cards.front: What is the captopril test, and what are its limits?
cards.back: Acute captopril blockade of Ang II formation causes a reflex rise in plasma renin activity. The rise is much larger in renovascular hypertension than in essential hypertension. It was designed to avoid renal angiography, but it is only an adjunct test.

cards.front: Short note: Drugs that inhibit the renin-angiotensin system, by site of action

Aliskiren blocks renin, stopping conversion of angiotensinogen to Ang I
ACE inhibitors block conversion of Ang I to Ang II
ARBs block the AT1 receptor
Spironolactone and eplerenone block the mineralocorticoid receptor
Losartan, candesartan, valsartan, irbesartan, olmesartan, telmisartan and eprosartan

Diuretics and vasodilators raise renin by lowering BP
NSAIDs and COX-2 inhibitors lower renin release and cause salt retention
Combination with ACE inhibitors raises risk of hyperkalaemia and renal impairment

cards.front: Short note: Actions of angiotensin II and its pathological roles

points: Potent vasoconstriction, more than noradrenaline when given IV
Facilitates sympathetic outflow and noradrenaline release; blocks its reuptake
Spares cerebral, pulmonary and coronary beds relatively
Stimulates aldosterone release from the zona glomerulosa
Promotes Na+ reabsorption in the proximal tubule and reduces GFR and renal blood flow
Increases contractility; chronic action causes hypertrophy, fibrosis and remodelling
Drives hypertrophy and remodelling in hypertension, post-MI and heart failure
AT1 mediates nearly all major actions through Gq, phospholipase C and Ca2+
AT2 has opposite effects, such as vasodilatation and antiproliferation, but its role is poorly defined
Acts centrally to increase thirst and vasopressin release
Infused angiotensin II is FDA-approved as a vasopressor in vasodilatory shock

cards.front: Essay: Renin-angiotensin system - physiology and regulation of renin release

points: Renin from juxtaglomerular cells acts on angiotensinogen to form Ang I
ACE converts Ang I to Ang II, the main active peptide
Ang III and Ang IV are active; Ang (1-7) is formed by ACE 2 and tends to oppose Ang II
Circulating and local systems operate in vessels, heart, brain, kidney and adrenal
Prorenin binds the (pro)renin receptor and drives Ang II-dependent and independent signalling
Vasoconstriction and sympathetic facilitation
Aldosterone release and sodium and water retention
Growth, hypertrophy and fibrosis in heart and vessels
Intrarenal baroreceptor, macula densa (NaCl sensing with prostaglandins) and beta-1 adrenoceptor pathways
Long-loop negative feedback by BP and short-loop feedback by Ang II in the kidney
ACE inhibitors and ARBs raise renin by removing feedback
Diuretics, vasodilators, NSAIDs and beta-blockers alter renin release
Involved in renovascular hypertension, essential hypertension, remodelling and nephropathy

cards.front: What is captopril, and what does it block?
cards.back: A sulfhydryl-containing dipeptide analogue of proline and the first orally active ACE inhibitor. It blocks conversion of Ang I to Ang II and slows bradykinin breakdown. It does not block AT1 or AT2 receptors.

cards.front: Where and how does the direct renin inhibitor aliskiren act?
cards.back: It binds selectively to the catalytic site of renin and blocks access of angiotensinogen, so Ang I is not formed. This is the rate-limiting step. Renin concentration rises by feedback, but plasma renin activity falls, and Ang I and Ang II fall in a dose-dependent way.

cards.front: Classify: ACE inhibitors by chemical group
cards.text: {{Captopril}} is the sulfhydryl-containing ACE inhibitor, {{fosinopril}} is the phosphinate, and {{enalapril}}, {{lisinopril}} and {{ramipril}} are carboxyl compounds.

cards.front: Classify: active drugs versus prodrugs among ACE inhibitors
cards.text: {{Captopril}} and {{lisinopril}} are active without conversion, whereas {{enalapril}} is a prodrug converted in the liver to {{enalaprilat}}.

cards.front: Classify: angiotensin receptor blockers and the renin inhibitor
cards.text: Nonpeptide AT1 blockers include {{losartan}}, {{candesartan}}, {{valsartan}}, {{irbesartan}}, {{olmesartan}} and {{telmisartan}}; the direct renin inhibitor is {{aliskiren}}.

cards.front: Captopril: starting dose and timing with food
cards.back: Start at 6.25 mg twice daily in patients on diuretics or with CHF, then increase to 25 mg twice daily and up to 50 mg thrice daily by response. Take 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal.

cards.front: Why do ACE inhibitors cause cough, and what is done about it?
cards.back: ACE normally degrades bradykinin and substance P, so both accumulate in the lungs of susceptible patients. The dry cough is not dose related and usually appears within weeks of starting. It often needs the drug stopped, though it settles within days of withdrawal. ARBs rarely cause it and serve as a substitute.

cards.front: How do ARBs differ from ACE inhibitors pharmacologically?
cards.back: ARBs block the AT1 receptor directly and do not inhibit ACE, so bradykinin and substance P are not raised and cough is rare. They also block Ang II formed by non-ACE routes, giving more complete AT1 blockade. Ang II rises by feedback, so unblocked AT2 receptors are more stimulated. ARBs raise Ang (1-7) much less than ACE inhibitors do.

cards.front: Why are ACE inhibitors and ARBs contraindicated in pregnancy?
cards.back: They are fetotoxic. Exposure in the second and third trimesters causes fetal growth retardation, organ hypoplasia and fetal death. First-trimester exposure has been linked to malformations. The drug must be stopped as soon as pregnancy is detected.

cards.front: Which patients are at risk of acute renal failure when an ACE inhibitor is started?
cards.back: Patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis, or stenosis of the artery to a solitary kidney, because glomerular filtration in these kidneys depends on angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole. The risk rises with NSAIDs, diuretics and volume depletion.

cards.front: What is the mortality benefit of ACE inhibitors in heart failure, and how are they dosed?
cards.back: They reduce mortality by roughly 20% in symptomatic heart failure and slow remodelling, and they have long been first line for systolic dysfunction at all NYHA grades unless contraindicated. Start low, especially with diuretics, then titrate toward target doses; in the ATLAS trial, higher-dose lisinopril reduced death and heart-failure hospitalisation more than low dose. Sacubitril-valsartan was superior to enalapril (PARADIGM-HF) and is now recommended to replace an ACE inhibitor or ARB in NYHA II to III HFrEF.

cards.front: What are the pharmacokinetic and safety features of aliskiren?
cards.back: Oral bioavailability is very low because P-glycoprotein pumps the absorbed drug back out. It is mainly eliminated in faeces, has a half-life over 24 hours, and its BP effect persists for days. Adverse effects are mild (dyspepsia, abdominal pain, loose stools, headache, dizziness). It is contraindicated in pregnancy. Adding it to an ACE inhibitor or ARB in type 2 diabetes is not advised.

cards.front: Losartan: effect on uric acid
cards.back: Mild probenecid-like uricosuric action.

cards.front: What is the rationale and the main risk of combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB?
cards.back: Rationale: angiotensin II is also formed by non-ACE routes that an ARB can block, and ARBs cause a compensatory angiotensin II rise that an ACE inhibitor can limit. In practice the combination increases hyperkalaemia, hypotension and renal impairment, and trial evidence (ONTARGET) does not support combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB in hypertension, heart failure or nephropathy. Aliskiren should likewise not be added to an ACE inhibitor or ARB in diabetics (ALTITUDE).

cards.front: Case: a heart-failure patient on an ACE inhibitor develops a dry cough. Would you switch to an ARB, and would you give both?
cards.back: Switch to an ARB: cough comes from bradykinin and substance P accumulating when ACE is blocked, and ARBs rarely cause it. Dual blockade is not advised: trials (ONTARGET) show no added benefit and more adverse effects, including hyperkalaemia and hypotension. Check for renal artery stenosis, NSAIDs and volume depletion before the switch, because renal dysfunction is a risk with RAS blockade in these patients.

cards.front: How is nitric oxide formed, and what makes it unusual as a signal molecule?
cards.back: NO is made from L-arginine by nitric oxide synthase, using O2 and NADPH, with FMN, FAD, haem and tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactors. It is the smallest endogenous signal molecule and a gas at body temperature. It has no stored pool, diffuses across membranes rather than being exocytosed, and lasts only seconds.

cards.front: How do the constitutive NOS isoforms differ from iNOS?
cards.back: eNOS and nNOS are constitutive and Ca2+-calmodulin dependent, producing small amounts on demand. iNOS is induced by endotoxin, cytokines and TNF-alpha in macrophages and other cells. It is Ca2+ independent and produces large amounts over hours to days.

cards.front: Classify: nitric oxide donors
cards.text: Clinically useful NO donors include organic {{nitrates}} such as glyceryl trinitrate and isosorbide dinitrate, the organic {{nitrite}} amyl nitrite, and {{sodium nitroprusside}}.

cards.front: Amyl nitrite: uses and tolerance
cards.back: The only organic nitrite used for angina; it dilates veins and arteries, causes throbbing headache, and shows no nitrate-like rapid tolerance.

cards.front: What is the signalling pathway by which NO relaxes vascular smooth muscle?
cards.back: NO diffuses into smooth muscle and activates soluble guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP. cGMP activates protein kinase G, which lowers cytosolic Ca2+ (less Ca2+ entry) and reduces myosin light-chain phosphorylation, both by decreasing myosin light-chain kinase activity and by increasing myosin light-chain phosphatase activity. Actin-myosin interaction falls and the muscle relaxes.

cards.front: Which enzyme releases NO from glyceryl trinitrate, and why does tolerance develop?
cards.back: Mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase, which is abundant in veins and explains the venodilator preference of GTN. Continuous exposure generates reactive oxygen species that inhibit this enzyme. Tolerance develops within hours and wears off quickly off the drug.

cards.front: What is the mechanism and key toxicity of sodium nitroprusside?
cards.back: It releases NO (in red cells and other tissues, partly non-enzymatically by reaction with glutathione) and also directly activates guanylyl cyclase, dilating arterioles and veins equally. Its action is very rapid, titratable and brief, and nitrate-like tolerance does not develop. The cyanide released is converted by mitochondrial rhodanese, using a sulfur donor, to thiocyanate, which the kidney excretes slowly. High-rate infusion can cause cyanide toxicity (metabolic acidosis, arrhythmias, death); sodium thiosulfate or hydroxocobalamin is used for prevention or treatment. Prolonged infusion, especially in renal failure, lets thiocyanate accumulate (weakness, disorientation, psychosis, convulsions).

cards.front: Short note: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and nitric oxide

points: NANC neurones release NO in corpora cavernosa; NO relaxes cavernosal smooth muscle through cGMP
Sildenafil and other PDE-5 inhibitors block cGMP breakdown and treat erectile dysfunction
Sildenafil potentiates NO and lowers pulmonary artery pressure; drug of choice for PAH
Inhaled NO is first-line in neonates with severe respiratory distress and raised pulmonary arterial pressure; short-term benefit only in adults

cards.front: Essay: Nitric oxide - synthesis, actions, nitrates and therapeutic use

points: Formed from L-arginine by NOS using O2 and NADPH
eNOS and nNOS are Ca2+-calmodulin dependent; iNOS is Ca2+ independent
cGMP-mediated smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilatation
Inhibits platelet aggregation and leucocyte adhesion; antiatherogenic
Microbicidal action of macrophages through peroxynitrite; proinflammatory
Neurotransmitter or modulator in the CNS; NANC neurones release NO in erection
Relaxes the pyloric sphincter and gut smooth muscle

Glyceryl trinitrate (mainly venodilator), isosorbide nitrates (slower), amyl nitrite (no tolerance), nitroprusside
Continuous organic nitrates cause rapid tolerance

cards.front: Why does nitrate tolerance occur, and how do nitrates compare with nitroprusside in toxicity?
cards.back: Tolerance with GTN relates to its bioactivation by mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase being inhibited by reactive oxygen species from continuous exposure; it develops with continuous exposure and wears off within hours off the drug. Nitroprusside releases NO directly and its main toxicity is cyanide (with thiocyanate), a different problem from nitrate tolerance.

cards.front: What are the actions of the natriuretic peptides, and how do they relate to the renin-angiotensin system?
cards.back: ANP (mainly atrial) and BNP (mainly ventricular) cause vasodilatation, natriuresis and diuresis. They lower renin release, Ang II and aldosterone, counter-regulating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. CNP acts mainly as a vasodilator with little natriuretic effect.

cards.front: Classify: vasoactive peptides
cards.text: Vasoconstrictor peptides include {{endothelin-1}}, {{neuropeptide Y}} and {{urotensin II}}; vasodilator peptides include {{bradykinin}}, {{natriuretic peptides}}, {{vasoactive intestinal peptide}}, {{substance P}}, {{CGRP}} and {{adrenomedullin}}.

cards.front: Classify: receptors and their drugs
cards.text: The endothelin {{ETA}} receptor mediates vasoconstriction, endothelial {{ETB}} receptors release NO, and the {{NK1}} receptor binds substance P; {{aprepitant}} blocks NK1 receptors and is used as an antiemetic.

cards.front: Short note: Kinins (bradykinin and kallidin)

Potent arteriolar vasodilators via endothelial NO and PGI2; raise capillary permeability

cards.front: Icatibant: class, duration and main use
cards.back: Synthetic decapeptide bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist, resistant to kinin-degrading enzymes; acts for up to 6 hours after s.c. injection; used to reverse swelling in hereditary angioedema.

cards.front: What is the source and basic structure of cardiac glycosides?
cards.back: Digoxin is obtained from Digitalis lanata and is the only glycoside still in clinical use. A cardiac glycoside is a steroid-based aglycone (genin) with an unsaturated lactone ring, carrying one or more sugar moieties.

cards.front: How does digoxin increase myocardial contractility?
cards.back: It inhibits the membrane Na+/K+ ATPase from the outer surface of the cell. Intracellular Na+ rises, so Na+/Ca2+ exchange extrudes less Ca2+ and the sarcoplasmic reticulum becomes overloaded. Subsequent calcium transients are larger. The inotropic effect takes hours to develop because binding is slow.

cards.front: What are the early features of digoxin toxicity?
cards.back: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhoea, along with confusion, headache and visual disturbances. These extracardiac features usually precede cardiac toxicity, in about two-thirds of toxic patients. Further doses must be stopped at the first sign of toxicity.

cards.front: What is digoxin-specific Fab antibody used for?
cards.back: Fab fragments bind digoxin and related glycosides and rapidly reverse severe, life-threatening toxicity. They are non-immunogenic because they lack the Fc fragment, and are given by IV infusion.

cards.front: Classify: digoxin pharmacokinetics
cards.text: Digoxin is excreted {{unchanged}} in urine mainly by {{glomerular filtration}}; its half-life is about {{1.5 to 2 days}}, and it is a {{cumulative}} drug.

cards.front: Digoxin and other cardiac glycosides: plant sources and status
cards.back: Digoxin comes from Digitalis lanata and is the only glycoside in current use; digitoxin (Digitalis purpurea) and ouabain (Strophanthus gratus) are no longer clinically used; toad skin contains bufotoxin.

cards.front: How does digoxin slow the heart, and why is bradycardia more marked in heart failure?
cards.back: Digoxin increases vagal tone and directly depresses the SA and AV nodes, slowing AV conduction and prolonging AV nodal refractoriness. In heart failure, better output withdraws sympathetic overactivity and restores vagal tone, so the bradycardia is greater.

cards.front: Which factors predispose to digoxin toxicity?
cards.back: Hypokalaemia (a key precipitant), high calcium, advanced age, renal insufficiency, severe hepatic disease and thyrotoxicosis. Interacting drugs such as quinidine, verapamil and amiodarone raise plasma digoxin levels.

cards.front: How is digoxin-induced ventricular arrhythmia treated, and which drugs should be avoided?
cards.back: IV lidocaine, repeated as needed; it suppresses excess automaticity without worsening AV block. Quinidine, procainamide and propafenone should be avoided. Potassium is given for tachyarrhythmia only when potassium is low, and never with a high degree of AV block.

cards.front: Where does digoxin fit in atrial fibrillation rate control and in PSVT?
cards.back: In AF or flutter, digoxin slows the ventricular rate but does not restore sinus rhythm, and it acts slowly. Beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are preferred for rapid control, while digoxin suits AF with heart failure. In PSVT, adenosine, verapamil or esmolol act faster and are preferred to digoxin.

cards.front: What is the evidence for digoxin in heart failure?
cards.back: It relieves symptoms and reduces decompensation and heart-failure hospitalisation, particularly with low ejection fraction. The DIG trial showed no reduction in overall mortality. Digoxin does not reverse or slow the pathological remodelling of heart failure, and it can be withdrawn in some stable patients in sinus rhythm.

cards.front: Classify: factors that increase digoxin toxicity
cards.text: {{Hypokalaemia}} and high {{calcium}} increase toxicity; {{quinidine}}, {{verapamil}} and {{amiodarone}} raise plasma digoxin levels; {{thyrotoxicosis}} increases susceptibility to arrhythmia.

cards.front: Classify: management of digoxin toxicity
cards.text: For ventricular arrhythmias give IV {{lidocaine}}; {{quinidine}} and {{procainamide}} are avoided; AV block with bradycardia is treated with a {{temporary pacemaker}}; DC {{cardioversion}} is avoided.

cards.front: Which drugs raise plasma digoxin concentration?
cards.back: Quinidine (about doubles it: reduces tissue binding and renal and biliary clearance by inhibiting P-glycoprotein); also verapamil, diltiazem, captopril, propafenone and amiodarone to variable extents.

cards.front: Which drugs change digoxin absorption?
cards.back: Reduced by metoclopramide, sucralfate, antacids, neomycin and sulfasalazine; increased by atropinic drugs including tricyclic antidepressants.

cards.front: Digoxin dosing in heart failure: loading and maintenance
cards.back: Started without a loading dose at 0.125 to 0.25 mg/day; steady state in 5 to 7 days; increase to 0.375 or 0.5 mg/day at weekly intervals if needed. A loading dose of 0.75 to 1.25 mg over 24 to 48 hours is used only when an early response is needed, with close monitoring.

Low therapeutic index; extracardiac features usually come first
Stop the drug, correct potassium, give lidocaine, pace for AV block, and use Fab for severe toxicity
Heart failure with low EF, and rate control in AF or flutter
Not a first-line drug for PSVT
Ventricular tachycardia and high-grade AV block
Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome with AF, because bypass tract conduction can accelerate

cards.front: Case: an AF patient on digoxin and a loop diuretic starts amiodarone and then develops nausea and ventricular ectopics. Explain and manage.
cards.back: Three precipitants stack up: diuretic-induced hypokalaemia, an amiodarone-related rise in plasma digoxin, and possibly renal impairment or age. Stop digoxin, correct potassium (only if low and no high-grade AV block), and treat the ventricular arrhythmia with IV lidocaine, avoiding quinidine, procainamide and propafenone. Digoxin-specific Fab is for life-threatening toxicity.

cards.front: Which drug classes reduce mortality in systolic heart failure?
cards.back: ACE inhibitors or ARBs, or sacubitril-valsartan (which is now recommended in place of them); evidence-based beta-blockers (metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol, carvedilol, nebivolol); mineralocorticoid antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone); and SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin), the most recent addition, which reduce mortality and HF hospitalisation with or without diabetes. Diuretics relieve congestion but do not improve survival; digoxin reduces hospitalisation without reducing overall mortality.

cards.front: Classify: drugs in heart failure by purpose
cards.text: Positive inotropes include {{digoxin}}, {{dobutamine}} and {{levosimendan}}; loop {{diuretics}} relieve congestion; {{spironolactone}} and {{eplerenone}} are aldosterone antagonists that improve survival.

cards.front: Classify: vasodilators and the heart-rate-lowering drug
cards.text: {{Nitrates}} mainly dilate veins, {{hydralazine}} mainly dilates arterioles, and {{sodium nitroprusside}} dilates both; {{ivabradine}} acts on the {{sinoatrial node}} to slow the heart rate.

cards.front: Ivabradine: mechanism, indication and place in heart failure therapy?
cards.back: It selectively blocks the hyperpolarisation-activated (HCN) pacemaker channels that carry the funny current in the sinoatrial node, lowering heart rate without a direct inotropic or vasodilator effect. It is indicated in stable NYHA II to IV heart failure with sinus rhythm, heart rate above 70/min and LVEF 35% or less, when a beta-blocker is contraindicated or an adequate beta-blocker dose does not bring the rate down enough. Added to standard therapy, it reduced heart-failure hospitalisation and heart-failure deaths, but not total or cardiovascular mortality (SHIFT), and it lacks the cardioprotective effects of beta-blockers.

cards.front: Where do SGLT2 inhibitors fit in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
cards.back: Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin, developed as antidiabetic drugs, reduce mortality and heart-failure hospitalisation in HFrEF whether or not the patient has diabetes, and this appears to be a class effect. Dapagliflozin was the first approved for heart failure (USA, 2020); empagliflozin is approved for both HFrEF and HFpEF, and SGLT2 inhibitors are now considered first-line for HFpEF. They are added to the other prognostic drugs (ACE inhibitor, ARB or sacubitril-valsartan, beta-blocker and MRA). The mechanism is not settled: SGLT2 is absent from the heart, so natriuresis and glycosuria with preload reduction ("a better diuretic") is likely, with possible off-target effects such as sodium-hydrogen exchanger inhibition and less myocardial glucose use. They also slow chronic kidney disease. Adverse effects include genital and urinary tract infections and ketoacidosis.

cards.front: Short note: Inotropic agents used in acute heart failure

points: Dopamine and dobutamine give prompt, short-lived support, especially when BP is low
Tolerance and arrhythmias limit prolonged use; no long-term role
Inamrinone is an inodilator; its dose-related problem is thrombocytopenia
Oral inamrinone and oral milrinone increased mortality, so they are restricted to short-term IV use
Milrinone is about 10 times more potent than inamrinone and causes little thrombocytopenia
Sensitises troponin C to Ca2+ without raising cytosolic Ca2+; also opens ATP-sensitive K+ channels
Relieves symptoms in acute decompensation but does not improve survival
Hypotension may last days because of its long-acting active metabolite
Diuretics and vasodilators are the main treatment of acute decompensation; inotropes are reserved for selected patients with low output
No drug given during acute decompensation has improved long-term prognosis

cards.front: Short note: Vasodilators in heart failure

points: Venodilatation reduces preload and filling pressure
Useful in acute left failure with ischaemia; tolerance limits routine use
Arteriolar dilator that reduces afterload; useful with low cardiac index and modest CVP
Reflex tachycardia, ischaemia and fluid retention limit monotherapy
Dilates arterioles and veins; short-acting IV drug for crises, used with a loop diuretic and an inotrope
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate improves survival in severe heart failure in African-American patients on standard therapy
Also an option when an ACE inhibitor or ARB cannot be used, for example in renal insufficiency

cards.front: Short note: Beta-blockers and aldosterone antagonists in heart failure

points: Metoprolol succinate (SR), bisoprolol, carvedilol and nebivolol reduce mortality in systolic dysfunction
Start only in clinically stable patients at very low doses and titrate slowly; EF may fall before improving
Do not start in new-onset or acutely decompensated failure; if decompensation occurs on therapy, reduce or stop and restart after stabilisation

Spironolactone (RALES, in severe failure) and eplerenone (EPHESUS; also effective in milder failure) reduce mortality; given in low doses to all patients with symptomatic HFrEF (NYHA II to IV), added to an ACE inhibitor or ARB
Use low doses (spironolactone 12.5 to 25 mg daily) and monitor potassium; eplerenone avoids gynaecomastia
Finerenone, a non-steroidal MRA, is more selective and may cause less hyperkalaemia
Aldosterone drives sodium retention, hypokalaemia, fibrosis and arrhythmias
Roles in heart failure with preserved EF are uncertain
Beta-blockers are also indicated in asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction after myocardial infarction
Rapid up-titration causes hypotension, fluid retention and dizziness

cards.front: Why is hydralazine given with isosorbide dinitrate in heart failure?
cards.back: The combination is the only long-term oral vasodilator regimen with survival benefit, though ACE inhibitors and ARBs are superior. It suits patients with renal insufficiency or renal artery stenosis who cannot take ACE inhibitors or ARBs; it added survival benefit in severe African-American patients already on ACE inhibitor, digoxin and diuretic.

cards.front: Hydralazine in heart failure: which patients benefit and what limits it
cards.back: Afterload reduction in forward failure when cardiac index is below 2.5 L/min/m2 without a marked rise in CVP (below 18 mm Hg); limited by tachycardia, worsened ischaemia and fluid retention.

cards.front: Sacubitril: activation and PARADIGM-HF result
cards.back: Oral prodrug activated by esterases to sacubitrilat (neprilysin inhibitor); absolute bioavailability 60%; half-life about 12 hours. Combined with valsartan it gave a 20% greater reduction in death or heart-failure hospitalisation than enalapril in 8442 patients; common adverse effects were hypotension, hyperkalaemia and renal impairment.

cards.front: Essay: Drug therapy of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

points: Systolic dysfunction from coronary disease, infarction, valve disease or cardiomyopathy
Compensatory sympathetic, renin-angiotensin, aldosterone and endothelin activity becomes harmful over time, causing remodelling and fibrosis
Natriuretic peptides rise as a counter-regulatory response
Relieve congestion and low-output symptoms
Retard progression and prolong survival
Sacubitril-valsartan, or an ACE inhibitor or ARB
Evidence-based beta-blocker: metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol, carvedilol or nebivolol
Mineralocorticoid antagonist: spironolactone or eplerenone
SGLT2 inhibitor: dapagliflozin or empagliflozin, with or without diabetes
Ivabradine for sinus rhythm with heart rate above 70/min despite an adequate beta-blocker
Loop diuretics for congestion; add metolazone or spironolactone for resistance
Digoxin for persisting symptoms and AF rate control (fewer hospitalisations, no mortality benefit)
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate for selected patients (e.g. African Americans, or ACE inhibitor intolerance); vericiguat after a recent hospitalisation
IV iron improves symptoms and exercise capacity in iron deficiency
IV inotropes and vasodilators for acute crises only
Check potassium, renal function and BP after starting RAS inhibitors
Excess diuresis or vasodilation reduces output in preload-dependent patients
SGLT2 inhibitors are now first-line
Diuretics for fluid; control hypertension, treat AF and coronary disease; ACE inhibitors and ARBs may help, but most other drugs lack proven outcome benefit

cards.front: Essay: Inotropic and inodilator drugs in acute and advanced heart failure

points: Acute decompensation with low output needs support beyond diuretics and vasodilators
Inotropes are mainly for short-term use
Dobutamine and dopamine: beta-1 and D1 agonism; short benefit with tolerance and cardiotoxicity on prolonged use
Inamrinone and milrinone raise cAMP and cause vasodilatation (inodilators)
Thrombocytopenia with inamrinone; increased mortality with long-term oral use
Levosimendan sensitises troponin C and opens ATP-sensitive K+ channels
Hypotension is the main adverse effect
Nesiritide given IV relieves dyspnoea; no long-term benefit
Digoxin is the only oral inotrope in routine use, and it has no clear survival benefit
Sacubitril-valsartan (or ACE inhibitor or ARB), beta-blockers, aldosterone antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors are the long-term survival drugs

cards.front: Short note: Newer drugs in heart failure

points: Dapagliflozin, empagliflozin: reduce mortality and HF hospitalisation in HFrEF with or without diabetes; empagliflozin also approved in HFpEF
Probably act through natriuresis and preload reduction; genital and urinary infections, ketoacidosis
Neprilysin inhibition raises natriuretic peptides; valsartan blocks AT1
Superior to enalapril; recommended in place of an ACE inhibitor or ARB; never with an ACE inhibitor
Soluble guanylyl cyclase stimulator that also sensitises the enzyme to NO (like riociguat, but longer acting)
In advanced HFrEF after recent hospitalisation, added to standard therapy, it reduced CV death or first HF hospitalisation by about 10%
Symptomatic hypotension slightly more common
Non-steroidal mineralocorticoid antagonist (approved 2021); more selective, possibly less hyperkalaemia
HCN (funny current) blocker for sinus rhythm with heart rate above 70/min despite beta-blockade; fewer HF hospitalisations and HF deaths
In iron deficiency, improves symptoms, NYHA class and exercise capacity; after acute HF it reduced HF hospitalisation but not CV death

cards.front: Why is sacubitril-valsartan preferred to an ACE inhibitor in HFrEF, and what must be watched?
cards.back: In PARADIGM-HF sacubitril-valsartan gave about 20% greater reduction in death or HF hospitalisation than enalapril, so it is recommended in place of ACE inhibitor or ARB. Neprilysin inhibition raises natriuretic peptides while valsartan blocks angiotensin II. Hypotension, hyperkalaemia and renal impairment need watching. It was tested on top of diuretics, beta-blockers and aldosterone antagonists.

cards.front: Classify: endothelin receptor antagonists
cards.text: Dual ETA-ETB antagonists are {{bosentan}} and {{macitentan}}; the selective ETA antagonist is {{ambrisentan}}.

cards.front: What is PDE3, and where does it act in the cardiovascular system?
cards.back: Phosphodiesterase 3 is the isoenzyme that breaks down cAMP in heart, blood vessels and bronchial smooth muscle; inhibiting it raises intracellular cAMP.

cards.front: Essay: Phosphodiesterase 3 inhibitors in congestive heart failure

points: PDE3 inhibition raises cAMP in heart and vessels
Raised cAMP increases myocardial Ca2+ influx: positive inotropy
Vasodilatation lowers preload and afterload: an inodilator
Inamrinone (amrinone): bipyridine, selective PDE3 inhibitor
Milrinone: more selective, at least 10 times more potent, half-life about 80 min
Levosimendan also inhibits PDE3, besides troponin C sensitisation
Inamrinone: dose-related thrombocytopenia, the most prominent problem
Also nausea, diarrhoea, liver damage, fever and arrhythmias
Milrinone causes little thrombocytopenia
Short-term IV use only in severe, refractory CHF
Added to digoxin, diuretics and vasodilators
Milrinone dose: 50 µg/kg IV bolus, then 0.4-1.0 µg/kg/min
Oral inamrinone abandoned: efficacy lost and mortality up versus placebo
Oral milrinone also raised mortality in long-term trials

cards.front: Essay: Principles in the treatment of chronic systolic heart failure

points: Reduce mortality, hospitalisation and progression, not only relieve symptoms
Diuretics and vasodilators relieve congestion; prognostic drugs prolong survival
ACE inhibitor or ARB (or sacubitril-valsartan), with beta-blocker and aldosterone antagonist
Low-dose spironolactone or eplerenone (12.5-25 mg/day) to avoid hyperkalaemia
Beta-blocker: start very low, titrate upward, avoid in decompensation
Digoxin: symptoms and rate control, no clear survival benefit
Ivabradine when heart rate stays at or above 75/min despite an adequate beta-blocker dose
SGLT2 inhibitors reduce hospitalisation and mortality in HFrEF
Dopamine and dobutamine: short-term only, tolerance and cardiotoxicity
Oral inamrinone and oral milrinone: increased mortality
Stop beta-blocker during acute decompensation; restart gradually after compensation
Monitor potassium and renal function with RAS inhibitors and MRAs

cards.front: Cardiogenic shock: what does medical treatment aim to optimise?
cards.back: Peripheral blood flow, by tuning preload, myocardial contractility and afterload. Prognosis is poor when shock follows myocardial infarction.

cards.front: Short note: Drug management of cardiogenic shock

points: Restore peripheral perfusion by tuning preload, contractility and afterload
Prognosis is poor after an MI-related shock
Fluids may help, but rapid volume can worsen shock and cause pulmonary oedema
Diuretics and nitrates reduce preload
Dobutamine: beta-1 agonist, the usual choice
Dopamine: intravenous only, not for long-term use
Milrinone: PDE-3 inhibitor that raises cAMP
Noradrenaline, phenylephrine or mephentermine as an emergency measure for very low BP
Nitroprusside reduces afterload when BP can be maintained

cards.front: In cardiogenic shock, why can alpha-agonist pressors do harm?
cards.back: Reflex vasoconstriction is already intense, so further alpha stimulation cuts flow to kidneys and gut and raises the heart's workload.

cards.front: Dobutamine: receptor and main use
cards.back: Beta-1 agonist giving a positive inotropic effect; given intravenously in cardiogenic shock and acute heart failure, with dose titrated to response.

cards.front: Milrinone: how does it increase contractility?
cards.back: It blocks PDE-3, so cAMP is not broken down; contractility rises and vessels dilate. It has been largely replaced by dobutamine in shock.

cards.front: Essay: Cardiogenic shock - causes, goals and drug management

points: Mainly myocardial infarction; also sustained ventricular tachycardia or valvular and mechanical dysfunction
Poor prognosis once MI-related shock is established
Improve peripheral blood flow
Optimise preload, myocardial contractility and afterload
Fluids raise preload; diuretics and nitrates lower it
Rapid volume may worsen shock and precipitate pulmonary oedema
Dobutamine (beta-1) and PDE-3 inhibitors such as milrinone raise contractility through cAMP
Dopamine acts on renal and splanchnic vessels at low dose; high doses constrict vessels
Emergency pressors such as noradrenaline; reflex vasoconstriction limits alpha agonists
Nitroprusside helps when BP can be maintained
Chronic oral inotropes do not improve outcome
Advances beyond drug therapy are not covered in the owner books consulted; state this as a limit

cards.front: Short note: Polypharmacy in chronic heart failure

points: HFrEF needs drugs acting on different neurohormonal pathways
Standard therapy combines an ACE inhibitor or ARB (or ARNI), a beta-blocker and a mineralocorticoid antagonist
SGLT2 inhibitors are the newest class added to standard therapy
Diuretics relieve congestion but do not prolong survival
ACE inhibitor plus ARB: more harm than benefit (hyperkalaemia, hypotension, renal impairment)
ACE inhibitor or ARB with an MRA is formally contraindicated for hyperkalaemia, yet low-dose MRA is still given
Prazosin, or isosorbide dinitrate with hydralazine, did not improve prognosis in Caucasians; the pair is approved only for African Americans

cards.front: Aliskiren in heart failure or hypertension: how strong is the evidence?
cards.back: Its therapeutic value is unclear; it has not been shown to be superior to ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

cards.front: Essay: Renin-angiotensin system - pharmacology, limitations and recent advances

points: Renin cleaves angiotensinogen; ACE forms Ang II, which acts on AT1 receptors and drives aldosterone release
Blockade sites: ACE inhibitors, AT1 blockers and the direct renin inhibitor aliskiren; ARNI adds neprilysin inhibition to AT1 blockade
ACE inhibitors: dry cough and angioedema (kinin build-up), hyperkalaemia, renal failure in bilateral renal artery stenosis, contraindicated in pregnancy
ARBs: similar profile with less cough and angioedema
ACE inhibitor plus ARB adds harm without survival gain; aliskiren has no proven advantage over ACE inhibitors or ARBs
ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan): superior to enalapril in HFrEF; never combined with an ACE inhibitor or another ARB
Angiotensin (1-7) formed by ACE 2 acts on the Mas receptor; ACE inhibitors raise its level
Prorenin and the (pro)renin receptor add Ang II-independent signalling
